title: What a penalty does to the fit
hook: A curve hits every training dot. Add a penalty for wild bends: what happens to its miss?

knows: that a too-flexible curve can overfit its training points
that held-out points check a model
doesNotKnow: the standard cure of penalising large coefficients (ridge)
that the cure makes the training fit worse

misconception: A model that fits its training data worse must be a worse model.
objective: The learner can explain that a penalty on coefficient size gives up some training fit for a calmer curve, that held-out error usually improves at a moderate penalty, and that too strong a penalty loses again.

claims.text: The toy fits a degree-7 polynomial to 8 training dots drawn from sin(0.8πx) plus noise (sd 0.3) at evenly spaced x in [-1, 1]; 40 held-out dots come from the same noisy curve. 'Miss' is the root-mean-square vertical distance from dots to curve.
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (makeData, rms). Data set 1 is mulberry32 seed 1, the first seed, untuned; 'New data' steps through seeds 2, 3, ...

claims.text: Ridge chooses the curve that minimises the sum of squared misses plus λ times the sum of squared coefficients (the toy leaves the intercept unpenalised).
claims.source: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., §3.4.1 (ridge regression, intercept not penalised). Implemented by fit() in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: With no penalty the degree-7 curve passes through all 8 training dots (miss 0); any penalty above 0 moves it off them, and the training miss never falls as λ grows.
claims.source: 8 points, 8 coefficients: the interpolating polynomial has zero training error. Ridge training error is non-decreasing in λ (standard result; the penalised solution trades residual for coefficient size). Checked in the toy: training miss non-decreasing across the 7 λ values in all seeds 1-500 (script reproducing Demo.tsx). Data set 1: 0, 0.084, 0.128, 0.177, 0.260, 0.363, 0.502.

claims.text: In 490 of 500 toy data sets some moderate penalty (the best of five, 0.0001 to 1) beat no penalty on the held-out dots; the strongest penalty (10) did worse than the best moderate one in all 500.
claims.source: Seeds 1-500 of the toy, computed in the reveal by the same makeData/fit/rms that draw the stage, and by a separate node script (builder's; the fact-checker should re-run independently). Data set 1 held-out miss: 0.444 at λ = 0, 0.377 at λ = 0.01, 0.725 at λ = 10. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Wording note from the checker: the 490 counts the best of five lambdas, so 'a moderate penalty' became 'some moderate penalty (the best of five)'. Numbers unchanged; re-set to unverified because the text changed.

claims.text: Push to 10 and the curve goes much flatter: on data set N you saw held-out H at 10 against H0 with none, so too much penalty lost again (or, in the minority of data sets where it wins: still won here, though it usually loses). Values are the learner's own visit to penalty 10.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2. The 'loses again' part holds: lambda 10 is worse than the best moderate penalty in 500/500 and 10,000/10,000 further data sets, and beats no penalty in only 12%. 'Nearly flat' is loose: over seeds 1-200 the lambda 10 curve's range is a median 37% (16%-58%) of the training data's range, versus about 2.7 units for the unpenalised curve; it is strongly shrunk, not flat. Wording concern for demo-builder (e.g. 'goes much flatter'). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: Re-ran model: at penalty 10 the curve loses to no penalty in 441/500 seeds (88%), so 'loses again' needs 'usually'; and 'nearly flat' is loose (the curve is strongly shrunk, median about 37% of the training range per earlier check, not flat). Fix: 'goes much flatter and usually loses again'. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was 'nearly flat and loses again' (disputed: loses in 441/500 seeds, 88%; curve is strongly shrunk, not flat). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-ran model.ts from Demo.tsx over seeds 1-500: lambda 10 held-out miss worse than no penalty in 441/500 (88%) so 'usually loses'; curve range at lambda 10 is a median 37% of training range (95% range 21%-54%), 'much flatter' fits. | REVISED v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): The 'push to 10' sentence now quotes the held-out misses the learner saw on their own visit to penalty 10 (the gate requires that visit via the slider or the new 'Penalty 10' button), and branches on whether 10 lost to none on that data set. 'Usually loses' still rests on the 441/500 figure above. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own re-run of the extracted model, seeds 1-500: lambda 10 held-out miss worse than none in 441/500 (88%, 'usually loses'), worse than the best moderate penalty in 500/500. Reveal branches on big.held > big.none, and big is set by every visit to 10 (slider, button or New data at 10); the gate (too-much) guarantees a visit. Independence: the claim was first recorded by fact-checker (2026-10-13), but the sentence verified here is demo-builder v4 wording, checked fresh this pass.

claims.text: The held-out dots tell the other story: at penalty L on data set N you saw H against H0 with none (the visited moderate penalty, 0.0001 to 1, that did best against no penalty); if no moderate penalty was visited: on data set N the best moderate penalty, L, gives H against H0 with none (best of 0.0001 to 1 on the current data set, e.g. data set 1: 0.01, 0.38 against 0.44).
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2, computed by visit() in Demo.tsx from the same makeData/fit/rms that draw the stage; replaces the old 'H0 with no penalty, H now' sentence, which could quote penalty 10 after the jump. Data set 1 at 0.001: 0.41 vs 0.44 (r5 review screenshot). | REVISED v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. Quotes only states the learner visited. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Mod branch checked: own re-run seed 1 at 0.001 gives 0.41 vs 0.44 none; mod keeps the visit with the smallest held - none. But the stage makes a different sentence on a reachable path: from penalty 0, pressing 'Penalty 10' (or End on the slider) reaches both milestones without visiting 0.0001-1, so mod is null and the fallback prints '{none} with no penalty, {now} now' with now = penalty 10 (seed 1: '0.44 with no penalty, 0.72 now') as 'the other story', the bug the v4 change meant to remove. Fix (builder): gate the reveal on a moderate visit, or in the fallback compute and quote the best moderate penalty on the current data set (and record that sentence). | Builder fix (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): W-215: the fallback no longer quotes the current state (which could be penalty 10 after a jump); it computes the best of the five moderate penalties on the current data set with the same makeData/fit/rms. Builder run (node strip-types on the MODEL block): seed 1 -> 0.01, 0.38 vs 0.44; seed 2 -> 1, 0.42 vs 0.58; seed 3 -> 0.01, 0.32 vs 0.94. Gate unchanged (penalty-on, too-much). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Ran the MODEL block plus the reveal's fallback with node strip-types (fc23/pow.ts). Fallback output: seed 1 'the best moderate penalty, 0.01, gives 0.38 against 0.44 with none' (seed 2: 1, 0.42 vs 0.58; seed 3: 0.01, 0.32 vs 0.94), which matches the claim and the builder's run. The jump-to-10 path now quotes a moderate penalty, not penalty 10. The mod branch keeps the visit with the smallest held - none; re-checked. Advisory, not a dispute: the numbers are always true, but 'the other story' reads as 'held-out got better'. Two cases print a held-out miss worse than none. (a) The only moderate visit was a worse lambda, e.g. tapping the track at 1 on data set 1 gives 0.55 against 0.44. (b) The fallback lands on one of the 10/500 seeds where no moderate penalty wins (186, 200, 208, ...).

recall.question: Model A fits its training data perfectly. Model B, trained with a penalty on complexity, misses some training points. Which is likely better on new data?
options: B, if the penalty is moderate
A, because it has zero training error
recall.why: A perfect training fit often bends to fit noise. A moderate penalty trades a little training accuracy for a calmer model that usually does better on held-out data; too strong a penalty underfits.
